directions: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before the last frost, barely covering the fine seed, then transplant into lean, sharp-draining, slightly alkaline soil in full sun. This dwarf subspecies of common hyssop stays low and tightly mounded rather than upright and shrubby, making it far better suited to rock garden crevices, dry stone walls, and border edging than the taller species type. The same strongly camphor-scented, needle-like leaves and short spikes of blue flowers appear from midsummer on, drawing bees just as reliably as standard hyssop. Once established it tolerates poor, gritty soil and drought extremely well, and only needs a light shearing after bloom to keep the mat neat.

common_name: Marian Sampson Hummingbird Mint (Dwarf Scarlet Monardella)

planting.note: Set out rooted cuttings or container plants in fall to take advantage of winter rains, into well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun near the coast.

directions: Marian Sampson is a selected form of scarlet hummingbird mint noted for its unusually dense, low, wide-spreading mat and heavier bloom than seed-grown wild plants, making it a striking flowering groundcover for tumbling over slopes, walls, or the front of a dry border. Set out nursery-grown plants or rooted cuttings in fall in well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun near the coast, since it appreciates more moisture and shade than most of its sun-loving monardella relatives. The profusion of brilliant scarlet-orange tubular flowers opens over a long season from spring into fall and draws hummingbirds reliably to the garden. Once established it needs only occasional deep watering, and a light shearing after the main flush of bloom keeps the mat tidy and encourages repeat flowering.

planting.note: Root softwood cuttings in summer, then set plants out in fall or early spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun.

directions: Russian River is a compact, densely mounding selection of coyote mint originating from wild populations along California's Russian River, prized for tidier, more uniform growth than seed-grown plants along with a long season of soft lavender-purple bloom. Root softwood cuttings in a fast-draining mix in summer, then set plants out in fall or early spring into lean, well-drained soil in full sun. The strongly mint-and-oregano-scented gray-green foliage and abundant flower heads draw large numbers of native bees and butterflies through the warm months. Once established, water only occasionally during the driest part of summer, and shear lightly after the first bloom flush to maintain its neat mounded form and prompt a second round of flowers.
